strengths: Principled Complexity-Theoretic Formulation: The paper establishes a clean theoretical framework connecting context-bounded language models and agentic systems to classical complexity classes, offering formal separations between standard autoregression (TIME(O(S(n)))), single-context/constant-depth methods (SPACE(S(n))), and deep recursion (TIME(2^{O(S(n))})).

Thorough and Rigorous Proofs: The theoretical analyses in the appendices are detailed and comprehensive, providing two complementary constructions for Theorem 1 (direct TM simulation and an Alternating Turing Machine reduction using the Chandra–Kozen–Stockmeyer theorem) and a formal least-fixpoint semantics for general recursive agentic systems.

Clear Separation of Resource Concepts: Distinguishing local active space (bounded attention memory on GPU) from global storage (offloaded inactive call stack) clarifies why recursive scaffolding conceptually breaks the physical context-window bottleneck without requiring architectural modifications.
weaknesses: Unfair and Confounded Baseline Comparison: The empirical superiority of the 3B model over frontier models (GPT-4o, Qwen-235B, LLaMA-70B) is primarily driven by supervised fine-tuning directly on synthetic DPLL execution traces on the target task, whereas the baselines are evaluated via standard prompting. To isolate the benefit of recursive scaffolding, baselines should include frontier models equipped with the same recursive call/return scaffold, as well as tree-search or CoT baselines fine-tuned on equivalent computation traces.

Very Narrow Empirical Scope: Experiments are restricted solely to Boolean satisfiability (SAT), a problem whose canonical solver (DPLL) is by definition a recursive backtracking search. Evaluating only on SAT does not demonstrate whether recursive models can autonomously discover, decompose, and coordinate subtasks on more general multi-step reasoning, mathematical problem solving, or software engineering tasks.

Limited Algorithmic Novelty: The core mechanism—equipping an LLM with call/return tokens to push/pop context frames—is essentially identical to existing frameworks in the literature (e.g., Recursion of Thought, ADaPT, Thread, and RLM). The novelty lies almost entirely in the theoretical complexity formalization rather than in a new algorithmic or system design.

Practical Viability and Error Accumulation: The theory assumes deterministic, error-free token transitions, but neural autoregressive calls accumulate hallucinations and errors across depth. Furthermore, without an explicit memoization system, the theoretical total runtime can blow up to double-exponential in local space, a steep efficiency trade-off that is not thoroughly stress-tested in practice.

strengths: Rigorous Theoretical Formalization: The paper introduces a clean and mathematically precise formalization of recursive language models and recursive agentic systems, separating local context space (active attention window) from global space (inactive stack frames).

Principled Complexity Analysis: The paper proves clear separation theorems between standard autoregressive models (time-bounded), constant-depth recursion / summarization (capturing SPACE(S(n))), and deep recursion (capturing TIME(2^{O(S(n))}) via connection to alternating space/ATMs).

Optimality of Minimal Scaffolding: Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 nicely show via least-fixpoint semantics that arbitrary recursive multi-agent scaffolds cannot exceed the expressive ceiling of the minimal single-model call/return recursion mechanism under bounded active space.
Clear Presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written and structured, featuring clear conceptual diagrams (Figure 1), formal algorithms, and detailed construction proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: Confounded Empirical Baselines: In Table 1, the fine-tuned recursive Qwen2.5-3B model is compared exclusively against zero-shot/few-shot prompted frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.3-70B, Qwen3-235B). It lacks essential controls: specifically, Qwen2.5-3B fine-tuned on linear/monolithic Chain-of-Thought (e.g., standard sequential DPLL traces without call/return stack management) and fine-tuned on summarization-based context management. Without these, it is difficult to isolate whether performance gains stem from the recursive stack mechanism or from domain-specific supervised fine-tuning on DPLL reasoning traces.

Narrow Evaluation Scope: The empirical evaluation is restricted to a single problem domain (CNF-SAT / Boolean satisfiability), which inherently possesses an explicit recursive backtracking structure (DPLL). Evaluating on tasks where recursive decomposition is less trivial or requires fuzzy sub-goal formulation would significantly strengthen the paper's empirical validity.

Theoretical Foundation Grounded Heavily in Classical Complexity: The core complexity reductions (e.g., Savitch's theorem, Chandra-Kozen-Stockmeyer alternating space equivalence) are classical results. While their adaptation to bounded-context Transformers via the FASP framework is technically sound and relevant to LLMs, the conceptual jump from classical recursive TMs to recursive LLM call stacks is somewhat incremental from a pure computational complexity standpoint.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework: The paper introduces a clean complexity-theoretic formalization of context management by distinguishing between local space (active context window constrained by GPU memory) and global space (offloaded stack history).

Strong and insightful theoretical results: The proofs establishing that unbounded recursion unlocks TIME(2^{O(S(n))}) (EXPTIME for polynomial space) via alternating Turing machine simulation, whereas single-context models (including optimal summarization) are capped at SPACE(S(n)), provide a solid formal foundation for why branching/agentic architectures fundamentally outperform flat autoregression.

Unifying perspective on agentic systems: The least-fixpoint semantics and oracle Turing machine formulation for recursive agentic systems elegantly show that sophisticated multi-agent orchestration does not add asymptotic expressive power beyond the minimal call/return recursive scaffold.

Clear writing and motivation: The paper is well-written, with intuitive diagrams (Figure 1) and explicit pseudocode that clarify the distinction between autoregressive CoT, summarization, and recursive models.
weaknesses: Inadequate empirical baselines and unfair comparison: In Table 1, a Qwen2.5-3B model fine-tuned on DPLL search traces is compared exclusively against standard-prompted frontier LLMs from Wei et al. (2025). The evaluation lacks crucial controlled baselines, such as Qwen2.5-3B fine-tuned on flat chain-of-thought traces, or on summarization-based trajectories (e.g., Yang et al., 2025b). Without these, it is impossible to disentangle how much of the performance gain comes from in-domain supervised fine-tuning versus the recursive inference mechanism.

Narrow domain evaluation: The empirical validation is restricted to a single synthetic benchmark (Boolean satisfiability mapped to text puzzles), which inherently matches the recursive backtracking DPLL template used to generate the synthetic data. Evaluation on more diverse or naturalistic long-horizon reasoning tasks (e.g., multi-step mathematical problem solving, code generation with debugging, or interactive agent benchmarks) is absent.

Limited novelty in the recursive execution mechanism: The practical concept of equipping LLMs with recursive call/return tools or spawning sub-agents with fresh contexts has been explored in several prior and concurrent works (e.g., Recursion of Thought, THREAD, ADAPT, RLM). The novelty lies predominantly in the theoretical characterization rather than the system design.

Lack of failure mode and error propagation analysis: The paper briefly mentions error accumulation in the discussion (§6.3), but provides no empirical error breakdown (e.g., frequency of infinite recursion, invalid tool call syntax, unhandled backtracking errors, or context truncation when subproblem inputs grow).
